# The Cost of Intelligence, Episode 18: The #1 Search AI Costs a Tenth of the Runner-Up


### Spec Sheet Saturday reads the chip fine print, the AI trade falls off a cliff, Anthropic nearly gives back its pop, TSMC closes a door, and the top search model costs a tenth of number two.


[Strong Compute](https://substack.com/@strongcompute)


Nov 21, 2026


*Listen to this episode on [Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/2IxPM8PZTWFqI7dImuqyMC) or watch it on [YouTube](https://youtu.be/szJjoBzSGIQ) .*


Welcome back to


**The Cost of Intelligence** , our comedy news show about the money behind AI. Each episode, Ben Sand reads the industry’s invoice and asks one question: are you getting more intelligence per dollar?


This week: our first


**Spec Sheet Saturday** reads the fine print, so you don’t have to squint.


**The AI trade fell off a cliff** on Friday, and chip stocks bore the brunt. Turns out the market reads the bill too.


**Anthropic** gave back most of its debut pop on day two; the honeymoon lasted one night.


**TSMC** has stopped taking advanced chip orders from some Chinese designers.


**Nvidia’s suppliers** are building, slowly. And


**Google’s Gemini 4 Neon** tops Parallel’s web-research leaderboard at about a tenth of the runner-up’s cost. Plus three cuts from the Department of Token Efficiency. Here’s the written version, with every source linked.


---


## Spec Sheet Saturday


Chips, networks and power. Most maker numbers are an “up to”. That’s their best day. Yours will be slower.


**Memory.** Nvidia’s


**Rubin** , shipping now, holds


**288 GB** of memory per chip. Memory speed sets how fast the chip answers, and Nvidia’s own pages disagree: the


[Vera Rubin NVL72 rack page](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/vera-rubin-nvl72/) says


**19.2 TB/s** , the


[HGX server page](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/hgx/) says


**22 TB/s** . Two pages. One chip. Zero agreement.


For scale, the older


[H100](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/) holds


**80 GB** at 3.35 TB/s. Rubin holds more than three and a half times the memory and reads it nearly six times faster, even on the slower page (our math: 288/80 and 19.2/3.35). AMD’s


**MI355X** holds the same 288 GB at about 8 TB/s, so Rubin moves that data more than twice as fast (our math). Same size tank. Nvidia’s has the wider hose.


**Network.** Broadcom’s


**Tomahawk 6** switch chip moves


**102.4 terabits a second** (


[Broadcom](https://www.broadcom.com/company/news/product-releases/64031) ). Nvidia’s


**Spectrum-6** switch matches it (


[Nvidia](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-spectrum-six-arrives-in-gigascale-ai-factories/) ). Your Wi-Fi just looked at its shoes.


**Power.** Nvidia’s reference architecture says a full


**GB300 NVL72** rack needs


**up to 142 kW** (


[Nvidia docs](https://docs.nvidia.com/enterprise-reference-architectures/nvl72-ai-factory/latest/components.html) ). The average US home uses 10,791 kWh a year (


[EIA](https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=97) ), so one rack draws about as much as


**115 homes** , by our estimate. The homeowners association would like a word.


**Not shipping yet.** Nvidia’s


**Kyber** rack, with twice the chips of a GB300 rack, is due in 2027, Nvidia says, and it says its roadmap hasn’t changed. Analysts at SemiAnalysis reported in July that it has slipped to 2028 (


[Tom’s Hardware](https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/gpus/nvidias-kyber-rack-for-rubin-ultra-slips-to-2028) ).


Memory speed and watts set what your tokens cost. The spec sheet is the menu. The power bill is the check.


---


## The news: the AI trade cracks


As of Friday’s close (


[CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/19/stock-market-today-live-updates.html) ,


[Motley Fool](https://www.fool.com/coverage/stock-market-today/2026/11/20/stock-market-today-nov-20-stocks-plunge-as-ai-trade-unwinds/) ,


[Investing.com](https://www.investing.com/indices/phlx-semiconductor-historical-data) ):


-


The


**Nasdaq** fell


**5.3%** , the


**S&P 500**


**3.7%** , and the


**Dow** lost


**949.73 points** .


-


The


**PHLX Semiconductor index** fell


**10.7%** .


**Nvidia** fell


**14%** , closing at


**$125.53** .


**AMD** ,


**Micron** and


**Broadcom** each fell more than 12%.


-


For the week ended November 20, the Nasdaq lost about


**10%** , its biggest weekly drop since 2020, and the S&P 500 closed the week in a correction, more than 10% below its October record.


Why?


**Reuters reported** that SEC enforcement staff are examining Nvidia’s accounting, citing two people briefed; the SEC declined to comment. A probe isn’t a finding.


**CNBC** also pointed to profit-taking after Anthropic’s IPO and fears of more Fed rate hikes.


Investors dumped chips and bought paper towels:


**Walmart** and


**Costco** both closed higher.


*Per-dollar verdict: a cheaper chip stock is not a cheaper chip. If funding gets tight, data centers come slower, and your bill doesn’t get the discount.*


---


## Anthropic, day two


Anthropic closed its first day on Thursday at


**$97.17** , up


**17%** from its


**$83** IPO price (


[Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/anthropic-stock-dives-after-rip-roaring-ipo-095411951.html) ). On Friday, per the exchange’s daily figures the writers used, it fell as low as


**$83.05** , then bounced to close at


**$88.91** , down


**8.5%** (


[CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/20/anthropic-stock-ai-amd-nvidia.html) ). The low was a nickel above the IPO price. That’s not a cushion. That’s a coaster.


It’s been called the biggest IPO ever. With the extra shares the banks bought, it raised about


**$93.5 billion** gross, and about


**$91.6 billion** went to Anthropic (


[Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/news/ipo-close) ).


Anthropic buys compute by the gigawatt.


*Per-dollar verdict: a bigger wallet just joined the chip line. Hope it’s not standing in front of you.*


---


## The chip factory door


**TSMC** has stopped taking advanced chip orders from some Chinese designers, Reuters reported on November 19, citing two people familiar with the matter. It covers anything at


**16 nanometers or smaller** , unless the customer has a US export license (


[Taiwan News, via Reuters](https://www.taiwannews.com.tw/news/6478978) ).


The trigger is a Commerce Department rule that took effect Thursday and presumes those chips are controlled (


[24/7 Wall St](https://247wallst.com/investing/2026/11/20/tsmc-is-halting-advanced-chip-orders-from-some-chinese-designers/) ). The default is no. That leaves those designers on older processes, like 28 nanometers.


TSMC says it will comply with all applicable rules, but hasn’t confirmed the halt. No license, no wafer. Even the sand needs a permit now.


*Per-dollar verdict: fewer buyers in line for advanced chips. Your bill hasn’t heard the news yet.*


---


## Nvidia’s suppliers


On Tuesday Nvidia announced more supply commitments (


[Nvidia](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-expands-commitments-with-supply-chain-partners-to-support-ai-infrastructure-buildout) ). One is


**Kinsus** , a Taiwanese maker of chip substrates, the board a chip sits on. Kinsus plans to grow its Nvidia capacity


**more than 3.5x** , with the full boost targeted for the


**third quarter of 2028** .


Nvidia also has nearly


**$3 billion** in Amkor agreements, some paid up front. That’s


**under 1%** of the


**$390 billion** Nvidia has committed to its suppliers (our math).


*Per-dollar verdict: more supply is coming. Don’t spend the savings before the substrate ships.*


---


## A new leaderboard champion


**Parallel** sells web search to AI agents, and it ranks how well models use it. On its


[Search Capability Leaderboard](https://parallel.ai/leaderboard) (as of its November 18 update):


-


**Google’s Gemini 4 Neon** took first, scoring


**88.1** out of 100, at about


**$206 per 1,000 tasks** .


-


**Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2** came second at


**86.9** , at about


**$2,063 per 1,000 tasks** .


That’s about


**10x** the cost, which is how Parallel puts it too.


One caveat: Parallel built this test, and Parallel sells the search.


*Per-dollar verdict: the smartest model on this board costs a tenth of the runner-up. Check it against your own bill.*


All that to drive a future filled with


**Supply-limited Intelligence** , or SI for short. RSVP early.

## Department of Token Efficiency


Chainsaw fueled. Spreadsheets open.


**Cut one: reading scanned pages.** OCR turns a picture of a page into text. Daniel van Strien tracked the cost of reading 1,000 pages with open models on one rented Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 at


**$2.75 an hour** (


[his write-up](https://danielvanstrien.xyz/posts/2026/ocr-cost-trend/) ). In April 2025, 1,000 pages cost about


**$0.51** ; with the newest model it’s about


**$0.095** , roughly


**3 to 5 times cheaper** depending on image size. He found running models better saved more than new models did: a better setup made one model


**4x** cheaper. A million pages now costs


**$65 to $130** of GPU time. That filing cabinet in the basement? Now it’s a weekend project.


**The fine print:** it’s a benchmark run. Some models made up text on blank pages, and on dense old print the newest model only tied the April one.


**Cut two: leave the context alone.** Huawei researchers ran more than


**20,000** coding-agent runs on open models (


[arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22238) ). With cached input at a tenth of full price, adding retrieved code up front cut read and search commands but raised the bill


**33–42%** . Deleting old observations raised it


**38–116%** . Edit near the top of a prompt and the cached part behind it gets thrown away, and agents may take more steps. The delete key has a cover charge.


**The fine print:** it’s a research benchmark on open models, with API-style cache prices. Without a cache discount, deleting old observations saved


**19–36%** .


**Cut three: the model in your backpack.** Thinking Machines released


**Inkling 2 Mini** on Friday with open weights (


[Thinking Machines](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini) ). It takes about


**20 GB** , small enough for a laptop, and runs its middle layers three times for every token. On the company’s own tests it beat Qwen’s 27-billion-parameter model on most agentic coding tests while using about a fifth of the parameters per token. Its researchers ran it offline on a MacBook, and it built a flight simulator. A model on your own machine has no meter running.


**The fine print:** these are Thinking Machines’ own numbers. Qwen still wins at multi-turn chats, and looping doesn’t teach it more facts.


The Department of Token Efficiency. Read the meter, not the brochure.
